nameStory: The 'longhorn' in this grasshopper's name refers to its notably long antennae, which are longer than those of most other grasshoppers in its family. The 'band-wing' part comes from the distinctive bands or patterns visible on its wings when it spreads them during flight. It's also called the sand locust because it's often found in sandy areas where its coloration helps it blend in perfectly.
description: The Longhorn Band-wing Grasshopper is a medium-sized grasshopper with a mottled brown and tan appearance that makes it nearly invisible against sandy soil. It belongs to the short-horned grasshopper family, despite its common name suggesting long horns - the 'horns' refer to its antennae, not the short projections that give the family its name. When disturbed, it reveals colorful banded wings as it takes flight with a distinctive crackling sound. Adults typically measure about 1-2 inches in length.

idTips.label: Wing bands
idTips.description: When it flies, you'll see distinctive dark and light bands across the wings that flash in a striking pattern - this is your best identification clue

idTips.label: Sandy coloration
idTips.description: Mottled brown, tan, and grayish colors that perfectly match sandy soil - run your fingers through sand and you'll see similar color variations

idTips.label: Flight sound
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive crackling or rattling sound when it flies, unlike the silent flight of many other grasshoppers

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are noticeably longer than most grasshoppers - about half the length of the body when extended forward

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Stays very close to the ground and relies on camouflage rather than jumping away immediately when approached

habitat: Look for Longhorn Band-wing Grasshoppers in sandy, open areas throughout New England including beaches, sandy fields, construction sites, and sparse grasslands with sandy soil. They prefer areas with little vegetation where their camouflage is most effective. You'll often find them along coastal areas and in pine barrens where the sandy substrate matches their coloration perfectly.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active - eggs are still developing in the sandy soil from the previous year's laying.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults emerge and are most easily spotted, especially on warm, sunny days when they're most active and likely to fly.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, mating and laying eggs in sandy soil before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - the species overwinters as eggs buried in sandy soil, waiting for warm spring temperatures to hatch.

funFact: This grasshopper is essentially a master of optical illusion - it can remain completely invisible while sitting on sand, but the moment it flies, it transforms into a flashy display of banded wings and crackling sounds, then instantly vanishes again the second it lands and folds its wings!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other band-winged grasshoppers, but the Longhorn Band-wing's preference for sandy habitats and its specific wing pattern help distinguish it. Memory trick: 'Sandy homes need long phones' - sandy habitat plus long antennae equals Longhorn Band-wing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'longhorn' grasshopper, this species actually belongs to the short-horned grasshopper family (Acrididae) - the 'longhorn' refers specifically to its antennae being longer than typical for its family, not that it belongs to the long-horned grasshopper family (Tettigoniidae) which includes katydids.
compareHints: Since this is the only Psinidia species in our dataset, compare it to other band-winged grasshoppers in the Acrididae family. The Longhorn Band-wing is distinguished by its strong preference for sandy habitats, its relatively long antennae for a short-horned grasshopper, and its specific wing banding pattern that's visible during flight. Most other band-winged grasshoppers prefer grassy or rocky habitats rather than pure sand.
